prompt: Why does a phishing message reach an employee through a correctly configured firewall?
hint: What kind of traffic carries it?

choices.text: A rule for mail is missing from the firewall
choices.why: No rule is missing; mail is meant to pass.

choices.text: It comes as mail, which the firewall is right to allow
choices.why: Right. It arrives through the front door, addressed to a real person.

choices.text: It is encrypted, so the firewall cannot read what it says
choices.why: Even read in full, a well-written message looks like any other.

choices.text: It uses a port the firewall does not inspect
choices.why: It uses the ordinary mail and web ports.

prompt: Order these stages of the pattern, from first to last.
hint: The table in the section.
items: a page asks for a password, or a document runs code
software on the laptop contacts whoever sent it
the software reaches other machines inside
files are encrypted, or data copied out
trap: The foothold comes before the spreading: software has to be running somewhere before it can look for the next machine.

prompt: Match each stage to what the network can see of it.
hint: The last column of the table.

pairs.right: a connection to a name nobody in the company visited before
regular connections to one outside address, at odd hours
a workstation connecting to other workstations on file sharing
a sudden surge of writes to a file server

right_distractors: the firewall rejecting the message at the edge

prompt: Why does ransomware rarely stop at the machine where it starts?
hint: Where are the files that matter?

choices.text: It copies itself to be sure of surviving a reboot
choices.why: A copy on another machine is not about reboots.

choices.text: The first machine has too few files to encrypt quickly
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; value is.

choices.text: What matters is held elsewhere
choices.why: Right. The first laptop is almost never the one holding it.

choices.text: The firewall pushes it towards the servers
choices.why: The firewall does not spread anything.

prompt: desk asks the company's name server for example.com.login-verify.test. What comes back?
hint: Look at the status line of dig.

choices.text: REFUSED, as for a name the server is not responsible for
choices.why: That was the answer to open-resolver questions in lesson 6.

choices.text: NXDOMAIN: no such name
choices.why: Right. The browser has nowhere to go.

choices.text: The address of the company's shop, 192.0.2.80
choices.why: That was the answer for www.example.com.

choices.text: A timeout, because the firewall drops the query
choices.why: The server answered, with a status.

prompt: The query log shows 192.168.10.20 asking for www.example-support.test. What is that address to the defender?
hint: Why would a machine ask for that name?

choices.text: The server hosting the phishing page
choices.why: It is the machine that asked, on the staff LAN.

choices.text: Proof that the machine is running ransomware
choices.why: A lookup shows a click, not an infection.

choices.text: A source the firewall should drop straight away, since it asked for a blocked name
choices.why: It asked because a person clicked; the next step is a conversation.

choices.text: Somebody who received the message and clicked
choices.why: Right. The first person to talk to, who may have typed a password.

prompt: A name on the company's blocklist comes back with the status ___, so the browser has nowhere to go.
hint: dig's HEADER line.

prompt: Which limits of protective DNS does the section state? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two limits, stated plainly.

choices.text: A new lookalike is missed until somebody reports it
choices.why: Right. The list knows reported names; lookalikes are cheap to register.

choices.text: It hides which staff machine asked for a blocked name
choices.why: The query log names each one.

choices.text: A machine that uses a different resolver ignores it
choices.why: Right. Hence staff may reach DNS at the company's server alone.

choices.text: It breaks names under .test for everybody
choices.why: .test was chosen because nobody real owns it.

prompt: On which TCP port did desk offer remote desktop before its host firewall?
hint: The probe's second line.

prompt: Why can fw's rules not stop laptop reaching desk on port 445?
hint: Where are the two machines?

choices.text: The traffic never crosses fw
choices.why: Right. Both are on the same segment.

choices.text: fw's forward chain allows file sharing between staff
choices.why: No fw rule is involved at all.

choices.text: File sharing is encrypted, so fw cannot see the port
choices.why: Ports are visible under encryption; fw simply is not on the path.

choices.text: fw filters traffic to the internet, not to the LAN
choices.why: It filters between segments too, as the DMZ showed.

prompt: With desk's host firewall loaded, which machines may still open remote desktop to it?
hint: Read the saddr of the last rule.

choices.text: Any machine on the staff LAN, since 3389 is in the rule
choices.why: The rule also names a source network.

choices.text: None, because the policy is drop
choices.why: The accept rule runs before the policy.
Right. The management segment, where support works.

choices.text: laptop, whose connections come back as established
choices.why: Established covers replies to desk's own connections.

prompt: desk's input policy is drop and no rule mentions port 443, yet curl to the shop still works. Why?
hint: Who started the connection?

choices.text: The shop is inside the management segment
choices.why: The shop is at 192.0.2.80.

choices.text: The loopback rule accepts web traffic
choices.why: lo carries traffic from desk to itself.

choices.text: The replies match ct state established,related
choices.why: Right. desk opened the connection, so what comes back belongs to it.

choices.text: A host firewall filters incoming connections from other hosts, and a reply from the internet is exempt
choices.why: Replies are filtered too; a rule accepts them.

prompt: Why is the quarantine written with insert rather than add?
hint: Where in the chain does each put the rule?

choices.text: insert makes the rule survive a reboot
choices.why: Neither keyword saves anything.

choices.text: It lands ahead of every accept, so nothing desk sends crosses fw
choices.why: Right. An accept earlier in the chain would win.

choices.text: add would put it in the input chain instead
choices.why: Both name the forward chain.

choices.text: insert drops connections that are already established
choices.why: That is the drop's doing, wherever it sits.

prompt: How many packets had the quarantine rule's counter recorded when it was listed?
hint: counter packets ...

prompt: After the quarantine, desk's lookup of www.example.com also timed out. Why?
hint: Where is the name server?

choices.text: Protective DNS added the shop to its blocklist
choices.why: A blocked name answers NXDOMAIN, not a timeout.

choices.text: The name server is in the DMZ, reached through fw
choices.why: Right. The drop covers everything desk sends through fw.

choices.text: desk's host firewall drops DNS replies
choices.why: Replies are established and accepted.

choices.text: The name server quarantined desk by itself
choices.why: The rule is on fw, written by the defender.

prompt: Which of these does the quarantine rule at fw leave undone? Choose all that apply.
hint: The three things it does not do.

choices.text: Keeping desk away from the shop
choices.why: It did that: curl exited with 28.

choices.text: Keeping desk away from machines on its own segment
choices.why: Right. That traffic never crosses fw.

choices.text: Telling anybody that desk has been cut off
choices.why: Right. The ticket in the comment is how it is tracked.

choices.text: Counting what desk tried after it was cut off
choices.why: The counter did: 4 packets.

prompt: Which design keeps an infected client from damaging the backup through the network?
hint: Who starts the connection?

choices.text: Clients push to a shared folder on the backup server over an encrypted connection
choices.why: Whatever the client can write, the software on it can overwrite.

choices.text: The backup server fetches the data from the clients
choices.why: Right. Nothing inside may open a connection to it.

choices.text: Clients push to a folder that each one alone may write
choices.why: The infected client can still overwrite its own.

choices.text: Clients push at night, when nobody is working
choices.why: Ransomware works at night too.

prompt: In the terms of lesson 4's matrix, what does the backup server have?
hint: Row: what it may start. Column: what may start with it.

choices.text: An empty row and a full column, so every client can deliver its files
choices.why: That is the push design, the one ransomware can reach.

choices.text: A row to the machines it backs up, and a column empty except for management
choices.why: Right. The DMZ's shape, drawn for the opposite reason.

choices.text: The DMZ's shape, for the DMZ's reason: protecting the inside from it
choices.why: The shape matches; here the empty cells protect the backup.

choices.text: Both empty
choices.why: Then it could back up nothing.

prompt: Why should the backup system's administrator account be one the domain does not know?
hint: What does the attacker hold after taking the domain?

choices.text: Domain accounts expire too often for scheduled jobs
choices.why: The reason is who else holds them.

choices.text: The pull design requires a local account on each client
choices.why: This is about the backup system's own administrator.

choices.text: An attacker holding the company would hold it too
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It keeps the restore tests out of the domain's logs
choices.why: Logging is not the concern.

prompt: A campaign uses a lookalike registered yesterday, on no blocklist, and somebody clicks. Which control of this lesson still slows the attack?
hint: Which controls depend on knowing the name?

choices.text: Protective DNS, since lookalikes follow a pattern
choices.why: The list knows names somebody reported.

choices.text: Host firewalls that refuse file sharing between workstations
choices.why: Right. They do not care how the software arrived.

choices.text: The quarantine rule, which fires by itself at the first sign
choices.why: It is written by a defender when a machine is suspected.

choices.text: A push backup to a shared folder
choices.why: That design is the one ransomware reaches.

prompt: An accountant shares a folder from her workstation on 445. What happens when desk's host firewall is rolled out to her machine, and what does the lesson's reasoning suggest?
hint: Where do files live?

choices.text: Nothing changes, since 445 is allowed from the LAN
choices.why: File sharing is not allowed from anywhere.

choices.text: The folder breaks; add 445 from the staff LAN to her rules
choices.why: That reopens the door spreading software uses.

choices.text: The folder stops answering; move it to a file server
choices.why: Right. Files live on servers.

choices.text: The folder keeps working for colleagues whose connections are established
choices.why: Established covers replies to her own connections, not theirs.

prompt: A colleague wants to switch a suspected laptop off at once. What does the lesson recommend instead?
hint: What is lost when it is powered down?

choices.text: Isolate it, which keeps its memory as evidence
choices.why: Right. Powering down loses what is in memory.

choices.text: Restore it from backup straight away, before looking at it
choices.why: Restoring overwrites the evidence and learns nothing.

choices.text: Leave it connected so the counter can record more
choices.why: The counter counts only once it is isolated.

choices.text: Block its name at the protective DNS server
choices.why: The blocklist is for outside names, not staff machines.
